subject: Discrete Structures (Mathematics)
exam_relevance: 4-6 questions expected in BPSC TRE CS exam

questions.question: If A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {3, 4, 5}, what is A ∪ B (union)?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A ∪ B contains all elements in A OR B (without duplicates): {1, 2, 3} ∪ {3, 4, 5} = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}.

questions.question: If A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {3, 4, 5}, what is A ∩ B (intersection)?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A ∩ B contains elements in BOTH A and B: {1,2,3} ∩ {3,4,5} = {3}. Only element 3 is common to both sets.

questions.question: The power set of a set with n elements has how many elements?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Power set P(A) of a set with n elements has 2^n subsets. For A={1,2,3} (n=3), P(A) has 2^3 = 8 subsets including ∅ and {1,2,3} itself.

questions.question: The complement of a set A (denoted A') contains:

options.A: All elements in the universal set U that are NOT in A
options.C: All elements common to A and U
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The complement A' (or Ā) of set A contains all elements in the universal set U that do not belong to A. A' = U - A.

questions.question: If |A| = 10, |B| = 8, |A ∩ B| = 3, what is |A ∪ B|?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: By inclusion-exclusion: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| - |A ∩ B| = 10 + 8 - 3 = 15. The formula avoids double-counting elements in both sets.

questions.question: The Cartesian product A × B of sets A = {1, 2} and B = {a, b} contains how many elements?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A × B = {(1,a),(1,b),(2,a),(2,b)} — has |A|×|B| = 2×2 = 4 ordered pairs. The Cartesian product produces all ordered pair combinations.

questions.question: A set with no elements is called:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: An empty set (null set) has no elements. It is denoted by ∅ or {}. It is a subset of every set. |∅| = 0.

questions.question: De Morgan's Law for sets states: (A ∪ B)' equals:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: De Morgan's Law: (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B' and (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'. The complement of union is intersection of complements.

questions.question: A - B (set difference) contains:

options.A: Elements in B that are NOT in A
options.B: Elements in A that are also in B
options.C: Elements in A that are NOT in B
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A - B (or A \ B) contains elements in A that are NOT in B. For A={1,2,3}, B={2,3,4}: A-B = {1}. Also written as A ∩ B'.

questions.question: If the power set of set A has 32 elements, then |A| (number of elements in A) is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: |P(A)| = 2^n = 32 = 2^5, so n = 5. Set A has 5 elements. Power set has 2^5 = 32 subsets.

questions.question: The symmetric difference A △ B contains:

options.A: Elements in neither A nor B
options.B: Elements in A or B but not both
options.C: Elements in both A and B
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Symmetric difference A △ B = (A ∪ B) - (A ∩ B) contains elements in A or B but NOT in both. It equals (A-B) ∪ (B-A).

questions.question: For sets A, B, C, which of the following is a valid set identity?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: All three are valid set identities: A is distributive law (∩ over ∪), B is distributive law (∪ over ∩), C is absorption law. All are correct.

questions.question: A relation R on set A is reflexive if:

options.A: For all a, b, c ∈ A, if (a,b) ∈ R and (b,c) ∈ R then (a,c) ∈ R
options.B: For all a, b ∈ A, if (a,b) ∈ R then (b,a) ∈ R
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Reflexive: every element is related to itself — (a,a) ∈ R for all a. Symmetric means A implies B. Transitive means A and B implies C.

questions.question: A relation R is symmetric if:

options.B: For all a,b,c ∈ A, (a,b) ∈ R and (b,c) ∈ R implies (a,c) ∈ R
options.C: For all a,b ∈ A, if (a,b) ∈ R then (b,a) ∈ R
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Symmetric relation: if (a,b) ∈ R then (b,a) ∈ R. Example: 'is sibling of' is symmetric. 'is parent of' is NOT symmetric.

questions.question: An equivalence relation must satisfy which properties?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: An equivalence relation must be Reflexive (a,a), Symmetric (a,b→b,a), AND Transitive (a,b and b,c→a,c). Example: equality (=) is an equivalence relation.

questions.question: A function f: A → B is injective (one-to-one) if:

options.A: Every element of B has a preimage in A
options.B: Different elements of A map to different elements of B
options.C: Every element of A maps to the same element of B
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Injective (one-to-one): f(a₁) = f(a₂) implies a₁ = a₂. No two different inputs map to the same output. Surjective means every B element is mapped.

questions.question: A function f: A → B is surjective (onto) if:

options.A: Every element of B is the image of at least one element of A
options.C: Different inputs always give different outputs
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Surjective (onto): range of f equals codomain B — every element of B has at least one preimage in A. The function 'covers' all of B.

questions.question: A bijective function is one that is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A bijection is both injective (one-to-one) AND surjective (onto). It creates a perfect pairing between sets A and B. It has an inverse function.

questions.question: The relation 'is divisible by' on positive integers is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 'Divisible by' is reflexive (a divides a) and transitive (a|b and b|c → a|c), but NOT symmetric (2|4 but 4 does not divide 2).

questions.question: If f: A → B and g: B → C are both bijections, then g ∘ f is:

options.B: Also a bijection from A to C
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Composition of two bijections is also a bijection. If f: A→B and g: B→C are bijections, g∘f: A→C is also a bijection.

questions.question: The domain of the function f(x) = √(x-2) is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: For f(x) = √(x-2), we need x-2 ≥ 0, so x ≥ 2. The domain is [2, ∞). At x=2, f(x)=0 (defined); at x<2, the square root is undefined in reals.

questions.question: A relation R on set A = {1, 2, 3} defined as R = {(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,2),(2,1)} is:

options.B: Reflexive and Symmetric but not Transitive
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: R has (a,a) for all a (reflexive), is symmetric, and (1,2)+(2,1)→we need (1,1) which is there; check: it is transitive. So it's an equivalence relation.

questions.question: The truth value of p ∧ q (p AND q) is TRUE only when:

options.A: Both p and q are TRUE
options.B: At least one of p or q is TRUE
options.C: p is TRUE and q is FALSE
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: p ∧ q (AND) is TRUE only when BOTH p and q are TRUE. If either is FALSE, the conjunction is FALSE.

questions.question: The truth value of p ∨ q (p OR q) is FALSE only when:

options.A: Both p and q are FALSE
options.B: Both p and q are TRUE
options.C: p is TRUE and q is FALSE
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: p ∨ q (OR) is FALSE ONLY when both p AND q are FALSE. It is TRUE whenever at least one of them is TRUE.

questions.question: The implication p → q (p implies q) is FALSE only when:

options.A: p is FALSE and q is TRUE
options.B: Both p and q are FALSE
options.C: p is TRUE and q is FALSE
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: p → q is FALSE only when p is TRUE and q is FALSE. 'If it rains, the ground is wet' — only false if it rained but ground isn't wet.

questions.question: A tautology is a proposition that is:

options.A: Always TRUE for all truth value assignments
options.B: TRUE for some assignments and FALSE for others
options.C: Always FALSE for all truth value assignments
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A tautology is always TRUE regardless of truth values of its variables. Example: p ∨ ¬p is always true. Contradiction is always FALSE.

questions.question: De Morgan's Law in propositional logic states: ¬(p ∧ q) is logically equivalent to:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: De Morgan's Law: ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q; and ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q. The negation of AND is OR of negations.

questions.question: The biconditional p ↔ q is TRUE when:

options.A: Both p and q have the same truth value
options.B: p is TRUE and q is FALSE
options.C: p is FALSE and q is TRUE
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Biconditional p ↔ q is TRUE when p and q have the same truth value (both TRUE or both FALSE). It means 'p if and only if q' (p iff q).

questions.question: Which of the following is logically equivalent to p → q?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q (definition) ≡ ¬q → ¬p (contrapositive). Both A and B are equivalent to p→q. C (converse) is NOT equivalent.

questions.question: A contradiction is a proposition that is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A contradiction (absurdity) is always FALSE for all truth assignments. Example: p ∧ ¬p. Opposite of tautology (always TRUE).

questions.question: If p is TRUE and q is FALSE, what is the truth value of p → q?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: p → q is FALSE only when p=TRUE and q=FALSE. Here p=T, q=F, so p→q = FALSE. This is the only case where implication is false.

questions.question: The negation of 'All students passed the exam' is:

options.A: At least one student did not pass the exam
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Negation of ∀x P(x) is ∃x ¬P(x). So 'All students passed' negated is 'There exists at least one student who did not pass.'

questions.question: The inverse of p → q is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: For p→q: Converse=q→p; Inverse=¬p→¬q; Contrapositive=¬q→¬p. Contrapositive is equivalent to original; inverse is equivalent to converse.

questions.question: How many rows are in the truth table of a formula with 3 propositional variables?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A truth table with n variables has 2^n rows. For 3 variables: 2^3 = 8 rows. Each row represents one combination of T/F assignments.

questions.question: The formula for permutation nPr is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: nPr = n!/(n-r)! — number of ways to arrange r items from n distinct items where ORDER matters. nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!) is for combinations.

questions.question: The formula for combination nCr is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!) — number of ways to CHOOSE r items from n items where ORDER does NOT matter. Also written as C(n,r) or (n choose r).

questions.question: In how many ways can 5 students be arranged in a row?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 5P5 = 5! = 5×4×3×2×1 = 120. Arranging all n items in a row gives n! arrangements. Order matters in permutations.

questions.question: How many ways can a committee of 3 be chosen from 7 people?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 7C3 = 7!/(3!×4!) = (7×6×5)/(3×2×1) = 210/6 = 35. Committees are combinations (order doesn't matter — {A,B,C} = {B,C,A}).

questions.question: The Pigeonhole Principle states that if n items are placed in m containers where n > m, then:

options.A: At least one container must have more than one item
options.B: All containers have the same number of items
options.C: All items fit without any container having more than one
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Pigeonhole Principle: if n > m (more pigeons than holes), at least one hole must contain more than one pigeon. Example: 13 people must share a birth month.

questions.question: What is 0! (zero factorial)?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 0! = 1 by definition. This is needed for combinatorial formulas to work correctly. For example, nC0 = n!/(0!×n!) = 1, which makes sense (1 way to choose nothing).

questions.question: In how many ways can the letters of the word 'APPLE' be arranged?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: APPLE has 5 letters with P repeated twice. Arrangements = 5!/2! = 120/2 = 60. When letters repeat, divide by factorial of repetition count.

questions.question: How many 3-digit numbers can be formed using digits {1,2,3,4,5} without repetition?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 5P3 = 5!/(5-3)! = 5!/2! = 120/2 = 60. We arrange 3 items from 5 distinct items where order matters (316 ≠ 631). Without repetition.

questions.question: The number of ways to select 2 cards from a deck of 52 cards is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 52C2 = 52!/(2!×50!) = (52×51)/2 = 1326. Order doesn't matter (choosing {Ace,King} = {King,Ace}), so we use combination.

questions.question: How many binary strings of length 4 are possible?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Each position in the binary string can be 0 or 1 (2 choices). For 4 positions: 2×2×2×2 = 2^4 = 16 possible binary strings (with repetition).

questions.question: nCr + nC(r-1) equals:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Pascal's identity: nCr + nC(r-1) = (n+1)Cr. This is the basis for Pascal's triangle where each entry is the sum of two entries above it.

questions.question: If nP2 = 20, what is n?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.question: In graph theory, the degree of a vertex is:

options.A: The number of vertices adjacent to it
options.B: The number of edges incident to it
options.C: The shortest path from it to any other vertex
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Degree of a vertex = number of edges incident to it = number of adjacent vertices (for simple graphs). Both A and B define the same thing for simple graphs.

questions.question: An Euler path visits:

options.C: Every edge and vertex exactly once
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Euler path traverses every EDGE exactly once. Hamiltonian path visits every VERTEX exactly once. Euler circuit is a closed Euler path.

questions.question: A Hamiltonian path visits:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A Hamiltonian path visits every VERTEX exactly once. If it returns to the starting vertex, it's a Hamiltonian cycle (circuit).

questions.question: A complete graph Kn has how many edges?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In Kn (complete graph), every vertex connects to every other vertex. Edges = n(n-1)/2 = nC2. For K5: 5×4/2 = 10 edges.

questions.question: A graph has an Eulerian circuit if and only if:

options.A: The graph has at most 2 vertices with odd degree
options.C: The graph is connected and all vertices have even degree
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Eulerian circuit exists iff the graph is CONNECTED and ALL vertices have EVEN degree. If exactly 2 vertices have odd degree, there is an Euler path (not circuit).

questions.question: The sum of degrees of all vertices in a graph with E edges equals:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Handshaking Lemma: Sum of all vertex degrees = 2|E|. Each edge contributes 2 to the total degree (one for each endpoint).

questions.question: A bipartite graph is one where:

options.B: Two disjoint vertex sets, edges only across
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A bipartite graph has vertices divided into two disjoint sets (U, V) where every edge connects a vertex in U to one in V. No edges within a set.

questions.question: A graph is planar if it can be drawn on a plane such that:

options.A: All vertices are on the outer boundary
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A planar graph can be drawn on a plane without edge crossings. K4 is planar; K5 and K3,3 are not planar (Kuratowski's theorem).

questions.question: A tree with n vertices has how many edges?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A tree with n vertices always has exactly n-1 edges. This is a fundamental property: trees are connected, acyclic graphs with minimum edges.

questions.question: A tree is defined as a graph that is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A tree is a CONNECTED and ACYCLIC (no cycles) undirected graph. With n vertices and n-1 edges, it has the minimum edges to remain connected.

questions.question: In a binary tree, each node has at most how many children?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In a binary tree, each node has at most 2 children (left child and right child). BST, heaps, and expression trees are common binary trees.

questions.question: A spanning tree of a graph G is:

options.A: A tree that includes all vertices of G with minimum edges
options.B: A subgraph of G that is a tree and includes all vertices of G
options.C: A connected acyclic subgraph with no isolated vertices
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: All three definitions (A, B, C) correctly describe a spanning tree: includes all n vertices, is a tree (n-1 edges, connected, acyclic). Answer is D.

questions.question: A full binary tree with n internal nodes has how many leaf nodes?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In a full binary tree (every internal node has exactly 2 children), if there are n internal nodes, there are n+1 leaf nodes. Total nodes = 2n+1.

questions.question: The height of a complete binary tree with n nodes is approximately:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Height of complete binary tree with n nodes = ⌊log₂ n⌋. A tree of height h can have at most 2^(h+1) - 1 nodes. This is why binary search is O(log n).
